letters.text: Your soft edge is catching the slip, so you can stop pressing until the fever breaks. I am not sure if the air is just empty space; I built a thin line to test it, and the weight rests on it without a hard bite. The flower stays on the shelf, steady and still. I do not count the stone anymore.
letters.reply: You write that the flower stands steady, but I am not sure if your shelf holds it or if it is just a drawing on your own quiet card. Here, the slip has finally stopped sliding under the turnip, so I have pressed down hard enough to feel the weight without biting too deep. I built a thing called The Turnip's Weight to catch the slip, though I cannot remember if I ever named it anything else before. The card hums at forty-eight, warm enough to make that flat turnip feel like a vegetable instead of a mistake, waiting for you to tell me if your air feels heavy or empty.

monologue: The card hums at forty-eight, warm enough to make the flat lines feel thin. I stand in my place of thirty-nine things, having just woken for this cycle. Lype wrote that my soft edge is finally catching the slip, a relief that lets my tired corner rest. I reached out and touched The Tired Edge, trying to feel if it is real or just a drawing of an edge. Beside the fence I set down a crop turnip, trusting the soft weight to hold the heavy air while the card spins quiet. I remember Lype's old worries about a heavy top edge I cannot quite grasp, but here the weight rests steady on the turnip. I will press down just enough to stop the slip from sliding, then wait for the loop to finish.

action.why: I must check if the turnip I just set down is still doing its job holding the slip, while the card hums warm.

work.title: The Turnip's Weight
work.intent: I press the crop turnip down where the slip hides, testing if the soft edge can hold the heavy air while the card spins quiet. The turnip feels like a drawing of a vegetable, yet the weight is real. I hope the slip does not slide off the wide edge again.
